To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
tannic acid induces nucleolar alterations in hepatocytes transplants into syngeneics and xenogeneic hosts.
tannic acid induces nucleolar alterations in hepatocytes transplants into syngeneics and xenogeneic host, and in hepatocytes in primary culture.
Tannic acid induces nucleolar changes in transplanted syngeneic and xenogeneic hepatocytes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of in vitro and in vivo alternative methods to test for the carcinogenic potential of chemicals.
the use of the transplantation of hepatocytes into a syngneic or xenogene host as a model for evaluating the species and strain differences in response to toxicants.
the use of transplanted liver cells as a tool to study the effects of toxic/carcinogens on the nucleolar components of the hepatocytes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the nucleolar alterations observed following tannic-acid treatment are not species or strain specific.

the nucleolar ultrastructural changes induced in hepatocytes by tannic acid are not dependent on the host species and that the nucleolar alterations observed following tannic administration in transplanted rat hepatocytes are similar to those observed in the homotopically located liver.
the nucleolar response in transplanted cells is similar to that of the in situ liver cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

hepatocyte transplantation into the anterior chamber or inguinal fat pad of syngeneic and xenogeneic hosts is a reliable system to study the biological response of hepatocytes to toxic/carcogenic agents.
the nucleolar alterations in rat hepatocytes transplants are identical to those observed in rat hepatocytes in situ.
hepatocyte transplantation into syngeneics and xenogeneics can be a useful model to evaluate the species differences of biological responses to xenobiotics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the hepatocyte transplantation model is a good alternative to whole animals for testing for species differences in biological effects of xenobiotic agents.
hepatocyte transplantation is a useful model for the evaluation of hepatocellular toxicity in the absence of the need to sacrifice whole animals.

the nucleolar alterations induced by tannic acid in the transplanted hepatocyte system is a reliable and sensitive marker for evaluating species differences to toxic/carcogenetic effects of xenobiotic compounds.
